The covariation generator has no panel_conditions field to read. A sample series is detected from the observation text — three or more numbers in one sweep — and two series pair when they are the same length. Length is not comparability, which is why 37% of sampled covariation propositions set quantities of different kinds against each other.

1 pair(s) found at the pair stage did not become items: a spine edge whose two claims share one evidence node is not a pair, and ten such self-pairs were dropped across the corpus.

4The two-step items

Every item is exactly two steps: two observations the graph already links, asked so neither answers alone. Chains are these items joined end to end, in section 5 — never one long trace.

complementary — 4 items
nano_letters_com_o13_o24
step 1 · SAXS
Na SAXS contours stay nearly straight; I(q) curves overlap except a small drop at ~0.03-0.1 A-1 at 0.11/0.02 V
step 2 · ATOM:AIMD
Degree of oxidation at 2 ps ranks Li-Co3O4 (~91%) > Na-Co3S4 (~59%) > Na-Co3O4 (~36%); Na-Co3O4 plateaus after 0.8 ps
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about MEC/identification, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
Together, the near-flat Na SAXS contours and near-overlapping I(q) curves (only a small drop at q~0.03-0.1 A^-1 seen at 0.11 V and 0.02 V) rule out a large volume/structural change as the driver of Na capacity fading, while the AIMD-computed degree of oxidation shows Na-Co3O4 reaching only ~36% at 2 ps -- below Na-Co3S4 (~59%) and far below Li-Co3O4 (~91%) -- and plateauing after 0.8 ps, indicating the conversion/sodiation reaction itself stalls early. Combined, the structural-stasis result plus the low, stalled oxidation-degree result let the pair be read as favoring poor sodiation activity (minor conversion) over volume change as the source of Na capacity fading.
limits
  • SAXS alone only shows structural/volumetric stability; it excludes volume change as a cause but cannot by itself identify what does limit capacity.
  • AIMD alone gives a computed oxidation-degree ranking and an early plateau in a picosecond-scale simulation; on its own it says nothing about real cell volume behavior and does not rule out volume change.
  • The two measurements are different kinds of quantity: SAXS is an experimental scattering-intensity profile read at specific applied voltages (0.11 V, 0.02 V), while AIMD is a computed cumulative oxidation percentage from a picosecond-scale trajectory (2 ps snapshot, plateau after 0.8 ps) -- the simulated timescale is not the same kind of quantity as, nor directly comparable to, the electrochemical timescale over which real capacity fading occurs.
  • Only three AIMD systems (Li-Co3O4, Na-Co3S4, Na-Co3O4) are compared at a single 2 ps point, which supports a ranking, not a quantitative trend or rate.

claims n18

nano_letters_com_o15_o18
step 1 · XRD:synchrotron
Li SXRD: reflections at ~16.4, 19.2, 20.1 deg fade to a weak broad bump by end of discharge; none regain on charge
step 2 · XAS:XANES
Li XANES: discharged spectra lose the white line (~0.97) and match the Co foil shape; charged spectra differ from OCV
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
Put together, the disappearance of the oxide's Bragg reflections (~16.4, 19.2, 20.1 deg, fading to a weak broad bump by end of discharge, not regained on charge) and the collapse of the Co XANES white line (~0.97) to a shape matching the Co foil at discharge jointly identify the discharge product as a phase that has lost the oxide's long-range crystalline order AND has Co reduced to the metallic (Co0) oxidation state -- i.e., conversion of the oxide to an amorphous/metallic-Co-like product by 0.01 V. XRD alone only shows that the original oxide's crystallinity is lost, without saying what chemical state replaces it; XANES alone only shows that Co's local oxidation state matches metallic Co, without saying whether any long-range order survives. Neither alone supports the amorphous-and-metallic identification; together they do.
limits
  • Neither observation quantifies the fraction of material converted -- both are presence/absence (XRD reflections) or shape-matching (XANES white line, spectral shape) statements, not phase-fraction amounts.
  • The XRD broad bump does not by itself distinguish true amorphization from nanocrystalline Co domains too small to diffract coherently, and XANES (a local probe) cannot resolve long-range order either, so this pairing cannot separate 'amorphous' from 'nanocrystalline but XRD-invisible' Co.
  • On charge, XRD shows the oxide reflections are not regained and XANES shows the charged spectra differ from the OCV spectra; together these only establish incomplete reversibility of both structure and oxidation state -- they do not establish what phase forms on charge, only that it differs from both the discharged Co-metal state and the original OCV oxide state.
not identifiabletrue amorphous metallic Co versus nanocrystalline Co domains below the XRD coherence length -- both are consistent with a weak broad XRD bump plus a Co-foil-like XANES shape

claims n12

nano_letters_com_o16_o19
step 1 · XRD:synchrotron
Na SXRD: same reflections persist through discharge/charge with only modest intensity loss
step 2 · XAS:XANES
Na XANES: discharged spectra keep a strong white line (~1.25 at ~7728 eV), unlike Co foil; charged lie between CoO and Co3O4
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/fraction, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength conditional mechanism
key — the combining proposition
Together, the persistence of the same SXRD reflections (with only modest intensity loss) through discharge/charge and the XANES white line remaining strong (~1.25 at ~7728 eV) and distinct from Co foil, with charged-state spectra falling between CoO and Co3O4, jointly support that the crystalline oxide phase of PCO is largely retained on sodiation and that Co is not reduced to the metallic state. Neither observation alone rules out both possibilities: XRD retention of reflections alone would not exclude a small metallic Co fraction forming below diffraction detection, and the XANES oxidation-state signature alone would not exclude bulk amorphization of the oxide lattice. Combined, structural retention (XRD) plus retained oxidized Co (XANES, unlike Co foil) together indicate sodiation reduces PCO only slightly, without producing metallic Co.
limits
  • Does not establish the quantitative fraction or percentage of Co that is reduced/oxidized, or the extent of the 'modest' intensity loss in structural terms
  • Does not establish the mechanism by which PCO resists reduction, only that the crystalline reflections and non-metallic white-line signature both persist
  • XANES only places the charged-state Co oxidation state qualitatively between CoO and Co3O4 references, not a precise oxidation state or stoichiometry
  • The modest XRD intensity loss is not independently explained (e.g., disorder vs. minor amorphization vs. particle-level effects) by either technique

claims n15

nano_letters_com_o3_o5
step 1 · PHYS:N2_sorption
N2 isotherm: adsorption/desorption hysteresis from P/P0 ~0.5 to 1.0, uptake ~110 cm3/g
step 2 · SEM
SEM: agglomerated faceted particles (~250-500 nm) with open gaps; internal mesopores not resolved
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/microstructure/porosity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength associative
key — the combining proposition
SEM (F1d) fixes the visible particle-scale morphology: agglomerated faceted grains ~250-500 nm with open gaps between them, but it does not resolve anything smaller. N2 sorption (F1c) independently shows a hysteretic isotherm (loop spanning P/P0 ~0.5-1.0, uptake ~110 cm3/g), which by itself only says some pore-filling/capillary-condensation process is occurring somewhere in the sample. Put together, the two show that the porosity responsible for the sorption hysteresis is not simply the interparticle gaps already visible in the SEM image, since SEM explicitly fails to resolve internal mesopores at that particle size -- so the sorption signal must include a finer, sub-resolution porosity in addition to the coarse interparticle gaps SEM shows directly.
limits
  • The pair does not give an actual pore size or size distribution -- the paper's 5-7 nm figure is not obtainable from these two observations alone
  • SEM only samples a local field of view and cannot confirm that the finer porosity implied by sorption is present throughout the bulk
  • The isotherm gives an ensemble-averaged gas uptake; it cannot localize which fraction of the ~110 cm3/g uptake comes from interparticle gaps versus any internal mesopores
  • SEM's failure to resolve internal mesopores is a resolution limit, not evidence that internal mesopores exist at a specific size
not identifiablethe relative contribution of interparticle (textural) porosity from gaps between the ~250-500 nm agglomerated particles versus true intraparticle mesoporosity to the sorption hysteresis and ~110 cm3/g uptake -- SEM cannot resolve internal pores to arbitrate this

key — the combining proposition
Na SAXS contours staying nearly straight and I(q) profiles overlapping across cycling (only a minor, localized drop near q~0.03-0.1 A-1 at 0.11/0.02 V) indicate the electrode does not undergo substantial structural/volume change during Na cycling. Set against the severe capacity fade seen in GCD (discharge capacity falling from ~870 mAh/g at cycle 1 to ~480 at cycle 2 and ~70 mAh/g by cycle 40), the pair together supports ruling OUT volume change as the driver of the fade: if volumetric/structural collapse were responsible for the large capacity loss, the SAXS contours would be expected to evolve markedly with cycling rather than stay nearly straight. This licenses attributing the fade to a different, non-volumetric mechanism.
limits

  • The combination positively rules out volume change as the cause of the capacity loss but does not itself positively demonstrate that 'poor sodiation activity/minor conversion' is the actual mechanism -- that attribution is reached by elimination, not by direct evidence of reduced conversion extent in these two panels
  • SAXS structural stability and electrochemical capacity are different kinds of quantities (a scattering/structural profile vs. a cumulative capacity amount), so their joint pattern shows correlation-by-exclusion rather than a mechanistic link established by a shared measurement
not identifiablepoor sodiation activity (minor conversion reaction) cannot be distinguished from other non-volumetric degradation mechanisms (e.g., interfacial/SEI resistance growth, electronic disconnection) as the specific cause of the fade using only the SAXS structural-stability observation and the GCD capacity-fade curve

step 1 · XRD:synchrotron

the question, as the solver sees itDoes the upstream evidence account for the downstream observation about STR/phase/identity / PRF/service_capability? Say what the combination supports and what it leaves open.
generator spine_edgedepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength associative
key — the combining proposition
Taken together, the XRD Rietveld fit (Observation A) identifies the as-prepared PCO material as a two-phase Co3O4+CoO mixture (flat difference curve indicates good fit to this phase model), and the GCD trace (Observation B) shows this same material's 1st discharge exhibits a long plateau near 1.05 V reaching ~1330 mAh/g with a 1st charge plateau near 2.0 V reaching ~870 mAh/g. The pair supports that the electrochemical plateaus observed are consistent with lithiation/delithiation behavior of a Co3O4+CoO phase mixture, i.e., the voltage/capacity signature in Observation B is attributable to the phase identity established in Observation A rather than to some undetermined or single-phase material.
limits
  • The combination does not establish which phase, Co3O4 or CoO, is responsible for which plateau (the ~1.05 V discharge plateau vs the ~2.0 V charge plateau); it only shows that a two-phase mixture as a whole produces this profile.
  • It does not establish a quantitative causal mechanism linking phase fraction to capacity magnitude -- no phase-fraction-vs-capacity relationship is given, only a single paired observation.
  • It does not extend to cycling stability or capacity retention; Observation B is limited to the 1st discharge/charge cycle only, not the 40-cycle retention behavior.
  • It does not rule out contributions from morphology, surface area, or other unreported material features to the observed capacities and plateau shapes.
not identifiableContribution of the Co3O4 phase versus the CoO phase to the specific discharge (1.05 V) and charge (2.0 V) plateaus cannot be separated from these two observations alone.

key — the combining proposition
Taken together, the two observations establish that the specific material whose phase identity was confirmed as a Co3O4 + CoO two-phase mixture (flat Rietveld difference curve against the synchrotron HEXRD pattern) is the same material subjected to Na half-cell cycling, and that this material's discharge capacity falls steeply and progressively: from ~870 mAh/g at cycle 1, to ~480 mAh/g at cycle 2, to ~70 mAh/g by cycle 40. The pairing links a confirmed starting-state identity to a downstream performance trajectory for that same sample.
limits

  • The two observations are different kinds of quantity -- a qualitative/static phase-fraction identity versus a cumulative capacity amount tracked across cycle number -- so they cannot be regressed or compared as a dose-response relationship, only associated as identity-then-performance for one sample.
  • The severe early fade (870 to 480 to 70 mAh/g) is consistent with generic conversion-reaction electrode behavior; nothing in the pairing isolates the two-phase composition itself as the driver of fade versus other unexamined factors (e.g., particle-level or interfacial effects) that could produce similar fade in a single-phase Co3O4 or CoO electrode.

covariation — 2 items
nano_letters_cov_o13_o24
step 1 · SAXS
Na SAXS contours stay nearly straight; I(q) curves overlap except a small drop at ~0.03-0.1 A-1 at 0.11/0.02 V
step 2 · ATOM:AIMD
Degree of oxidation at 2 ps ranks Li-Co3O4 (~91%) > Na-Co3S4 (~59%) > Na-Co3O4 (~36%); Na-Co3O4 plateaus after 0.8 ps
the question, as the solver sees itAcross the series reported here, does the first quantity below move with the second quantity below? Give the comparison and say what it implies.
generator covariationdepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
Taken together, the SAXS data show that Na-Co3O4 samples keep essentially unchanged scattering profiles across cycling (I(q) curves overlap, with only a small drop at ~0.03-0.1 A^-1 near 0.11/0.02 V), while the AIMD data show that the conversion (oxidation) reaction for Na-Co3O4 reaches only ~36% by 2 ps and plateaus after 0.8 ps, well below Li-Co3O4's ~91% and Na-Co3S4's ~59%. Combined, the SAXS observation argues against a volume/structural-change mechanism for Na capacity fading, while the AIMD observation identifies a restricted, early-saturating conversion extent for Na-Co3O4. Put together they support attributing Na capacity fading to limited sodiation (conversion) activity rather than to volume change.
limits
  • SAXS alone shows the absence of structural change but does not by itself identify what limits capacity, so it cannot support the 'poor sodiation activity' half of the claim without the AIMD data
  • AIMD alone shows a low, early-plateauing oxidation extent for Na-Co3O4 but does not by itself rule out volume change as a contributing mechanism, so it cannot support the 'not volume change' half of the claim without the SAXS data
  • the two observations come from different domains indexed differently: SAXS is an experimental measurement indexed by applied voltage (0.11 V, 0.02 V), while AIMD is a computational simulation indexed by simulated time (up to 2 ps, plateau at 0.8 ps); no direct correspondence between these voltage points and time points is established
  • the AIMD comparison spans three different material systems (Li-Co3O4, Na-Co3S4, Na-Co3O4) on a picosecond simulation timescale, which is not the same timescale as the electrochemical cycling probed by SAXS
  • both observations are indirect proxies (scattering-curve shape; simulated oxidation fraction) rather than direct measurements of capacity fade, so the link to actual capacity loss is inferential

key — the combining proposition
The type IV adsorption/desorption hysteresis (P/P0 ~0.5 to 1.0, uptake ~110 cm3/g) together with the pore-size-distribution peaks at ~5.5 and ~6.9 nm (with a tail below 4 nm) jointly support that PCO is mesoporous with pores mostly in the 5-7 nm range: the hysteresis shape signals that mesopores are present, and the PSD peaks locate where in the size range those pores actually fall.
limits
  • The pore-size distribution shown in the inset is conventionally computed from the same adsorption/desorption isotherm (e.g. via BJH-type analysis), so B is not an independent confirmation of A -- both come from one measurement on one panel (F1c), and the observed peaks are numerically derived from the same curve that produced the hysteresis.
  • Together they characterize a single sample's pore structure; they do not establish a trend or comparison across a series, since no second condition or sample is described here.
  • The tail below 4 nm hints at some smaller mesopores/micropores but the isotherm shape and the two cited peak values do not quantify or separate that contribution.
  • Neither observation gives surface area, total pore volume, or particle-level structure -- only the qualitative isotherm type and the two headline PSD peak positions are available.
